Section heading.
Saves go to a holding branch; visitors see content only after a deliberate publish and the site deploy.
The roster of admin authors is small and owner-curated.
The realistic risks are session handling, endpoint abuse, and a leaked commit credential.
Under an identity gate the realistic risk moves to JWT verification, gate scope, and email verification.

Caption: the repository marks where this model ends and render safety begins.
Section heading.
These sections describe the built-in sign-in, which an identity gate replaces entirely.
A single-use token is stored as a SHA-256 hash and emailed as a link.
The session is stored the same way, by hash rather than the raw value.
Token lifetime ten minutes, session lifetime thirty days, one send per address per minute.
None of the three constants can be loosened through the adapter.
There is no password in the sign-in path.
No third-party identity provider is involved; sign-in proves only editor-table membership.
An address not on the roster gets the same sent outcome a real editor gets.
A repeat request inside the cooldown returns a distinct throttled status that reveals roster membership.
The throttled signal is an accepted trade to spare an editor a flooded inbox.
Section heading.
The login load leaves a nonce in the pending-login cookie and the request action reuses it.
Confirm compares the nonce hash inside the same atomic DELETE that consumes the token.
The cookie outlives the token but grants nothing once the row expires.
A late click arrives with the cookie and reads that the link expired.
The binding closes a login-CSRF where an attacker link lands the editor in the attacker session.
The binding stops a link-following mail scanner from spending the link.
The comparison is the consuming DELETE predicate, so a wrong-browser click burns nothing.
A confirm with no cookie passes NULL; a bound row survives and an unbound row still signs in.
Only a bound row refusal takes the distinct no-pending-request code.
The code has its own page copy naming this browser missing pending sign-in.
The engine exports the code as NO_PENDING_REQUEST_ERROR for a site own login page.
A throttled repeat request moves the live token binding to the requesting browser.
The rebind sends no new token or email and leaves the cooldown where it was.
Rationale that the binding alone is a lockout an attacker could keep re-applying.
Last-requester-wins is safe because asking alone grants nothing.
A fresh request already replaced the previous token before the binding existed.
Recovery is asking again, and the rebind treats requesters symmetrically.
A holder of a forwarded token can rebind it inside the cooldown, so forwarding hands over an account.
The rebind skips an expired row and an unbound row and is a single UPDATE.
A rebind racing the confirm loses cleanly whichever statement lands first.
A row with a NULL nonce hash confirms from any browser.
Older engines, the bootstrap INSERT, and hand-seeded recovery rows write unbound rows.
The request action writes a binding every time, so unbound rows never occur in steady state.
An unbound row is a link a mail scanner can spend during its ten minutes.
A link opened in a different browser than the one that asked is refused.
Integrity is judged worth more than the convenience of opening a link elsewhere.
The nonce hash column comes from migration 0004, which must be applied before deploying.
No command checks the column, so a missed migration fails the first sign-in.
The nonce column allows NULL, so an emailed link survives the migration.
Section heading.
The session cookie takes the __Host- prefix on every https deploy and drops it on local http.
The session cookie derives Secure through the same rule as the CSRF cookie.
The CSRF cookie follows the same __Host- and Secure rules as the session cookie.
A monotonic Secure rule: https always Secure, local hosts bare, otherwise PUBLIC_ORIGIN decides.
Logout deletes both name forms of both cookies.
The CSRF cookie is HttpOnly, Path slash, SameSite Lax set explicitly, with a thirty-day Max-Age.
The CSRF cookie refreshes its Max-Age at every issue; the session lifetime counts from sign-in.
The CSRF value rotates only at login and logout on the magic-link path.
A re-authentication through the confirm path can give another open tab one recoverable 403.
Under an identity gate, cairn has no login event to attach a rotation to.
The identity option replaces the whole magic-link sign-in with a site-supplied gate.
Cairn mints no token or session and looks the proven email up in the roster.
Under identity the effective session lifetime moves to the gate, 24 hours by default.
Set the Access session to hours because cairn has no independent timeout.
The guard reads identity.resolve instead of a session cookie under identity.
The session cookie is still read on logout and on a CSRF rejection, never to authenticate.
A CSRF rejection reads the session cookie only to set the presence flag.
A stale magic-link session cookie never authenticates a request under identity.
hasSession on a CSRF rejection is always false under identity.
Rationale for not resolving identity ahead of the CSRF check on rejected posts.
CSRF runs before session or identity resolution, so identity.resolve never runs on a refused request.
Under identity the CSRF cookie mints on the first admin request and persists across identity changes.
On a shared browser a second editor inherits the first editor CSRF token.
A deliberate sign-out through cairn logout clears the CSRF cookie.
A short Access session narrows the exploit window but neither lever closes it.
The email the gate proves is the sole link between gate and roster.
Enable only a login method that proves control of the asserted address.
Pointer to the sign-in page for the full login-method guidance.
The gate proves identity only on hostnames its application covers; another hostname admits any valid token.
Close the workers.dev and preview hostnames and confirm every custom hostname is gated.
No tool checks the workers.dev exposure gap yet; check both hostnames by hand.
Seed the first owner out of band before enabling identity, since the guard performs no bootstrap write.
SvelteKit default CSRF check compares Origin with the site origin, as one global switch.
A privacy-hardened browser can send no Origin on a legitimate same-origin form post.
A site sets csrf checkOrigin false in svelte.config.js to hand the authority to the guard.
checkOrigin is deprecated in favor of trustedOrigins but stays supported across the tested range.
Pointer to the supported toolchain reference.
The guard enforces an Origin-independent double-submit token compared in constant time.
Outside /admin the guard restores the framework Origin check the site disabled.
createAuthGuard is the handle hook and every request passes through it in a fixed order.
Step 1 refuses closed when a deployed runtime carries the local-only flag.
Step 2 restores the Origin check outside /admin.
Step 3 shows a help page for /admin requests over plain http on non-local hosts.
Step 4 names a condition when the AUTH_DB binding is missing.
Step 5 accepts the double-submit field or a custom header.
Step 6 attaches locals.cairnEditor and locals.cairnAccess.
A site configuring identity replaces step 6 with the gate own resolution.
Every refusing step but step 6 logs a named guard.refused reason.
A missing session redirects to login without logging; identity refusals are logged.
CAIRN_DEV_BACKEND is refused in two places on different terms from one shared module.
Only 1 and boolean true count as set, in either env source.
Both places read platform.env and process.env.
The guard refuses on the flag alone, as it is mounted only in production builds.
The channel actions refuse only when the flag is set and the request is deployed, before other work.
The deployed-runtime test reads PUBLIC_ORIGIN before the request, moving only toward refusing.
The tripwire cannot see a dev-shaped transport deployed with the flag unset.
A dev-branch bundle that replaces the guard sits outside both refusals.
CI greps a wrangler dry-run of a default build for dev-only markers.
A role string resolves to one of three capabilities through the declared role vocabulary.
A zero-config site gets the built-in owner and editor pair.
Capability alone gates the engine own screens.
The guard and the nav share one access declaration, so an unreachable route is absent from the nav.
requireAccess with no map entry refuses every session, owner included.
The engine screens read the map permissively.
A site own POST actions read the map fail-closed.
A declared map narrows only the targets it names; only a none session is refused everywhere.
canReach is the one function deciding route enforcement and nav visibility.
An unmapped target still lets an editor save, publish, delete, upload, and change settings.
The site-wide publish is open to any editor session and filters by canReach per concept.
The tidy and dictionary actions check access only when a concept parameter is present.
Deny-by-default needs a rule for every concept plus the four fixed engine screens.
Snippet declaring an exhaustive access map.
An exhaustive map closes the site-wide publish residual.
Composition warns with config.access_unmapped when a map covers only some targets.
Heading: ownerOnly stacks on top of the access map.
Other pages link here rather than restating the rule.
ownerOnly requires owner capability in addition to the map rule and only narrows.
A target with no map rule refuses even an owner-only call.
For a non-owner both the role list and the owner requirement must pass.
This ownerOnly differs from the cosmetic one a navLayout entry carries.
authorizeAdminTarget is fail-closed at three ordered gates.
An unmapped target is refused here, opposite to canReach, because the action opted into the map.
createSectionAction and createAdminAction refuse with 403 through different channels and audit the refusal.
Every admin response carries the fixed security headers and Cache-Control private, no-store.
A rejection response sends no HSTS header at all.
Mount every token-issuing load under /admin since the headers apply only there.
no-referrer is scoped to /admin, never a site-wide default.
A blanket no-referrer strips Origin from a same-origin form POST so it arrives as null.
originMatches stays a strict compare and rejects an Origin null request outside /admin.
cairn doctor flags a blanket no-referrer heuristically.
no-referrer is safe on /admin because its CSRF protection is the double-submit token.
Non-admin routes and every createAuthChannel action rely on the origin compare alone.
Serve strict-origin-when-cross-origin or same-origin and scope no-referrer to double-submit routes.
The same-origin policy still drops Referer cross-origin but keeps the true Origin on same-origin POSTs.
Section heading.
/admin carries no full Content-Security-Policy.
The nonce machinery a correct CSP needs threads through the site own SvelteKit config.
The threat a CSP would add coverage for is low value against git-audited content.
The reasoning assumes the roster; under identity the admitted population can be broader.
The XSS surface that matters is governed on the public render path.
